name: Helium Atom
description: Helium: 2 protons, 2 neutrons, 2 electrons (spin up and spin down in 1s)

layman.title: Two of Everything
layman.summary: Helium — the atom that makes balloons float and voices squeaky

sections.whatsHappening: You're looking at a helium atom — the second simplest element. Its nucleus contains 2 protons (red) and 2 neutrons (gray), tightly bound together by the strong nuclear force. Two electrons share the same orbital cloud around the nucleus, but with opposite spins — this is required by the Pauli exclusion principle, which says no two electrons (or other identical fermions) can be in exactly the same quantum state.
sections.whyItMatters: Helium is the second most abundant element in the universe (after hydrogen). Most of it was made in the first few minutes after the Big Bang; stars have added a little more since, by nuclear fusion. On Earth, we find it trapped underground, made by the radioactive decay of uranium and thorium. Once it escapes into the atmosphere, it's light enough to float away into space forever. That's why helium is actually a non-renewable resource!
sections.whatToWatch: Notice the nucleus has four particles clustered tightly together — two red protons and two gray neutrons. The blue electron cloud surrounds them. Both electrons occupy the same 1s orbital, but they must have opposite spins (+1/2 and -1/2) to coexist.
sections.funFact: Helium was discovered on the Sun before it was found on Earth! In 1868, astronomers saw an unknown spectral line in sunlight and named the mystery element 'helium' after Helios, the Greek sun god. It wasn't found on Earth until 27 years later.

scientific.narrative: The helium atom has atomic number Z=2 with a nucleus of 2 protons and 2 neutrons (helium-4, the most common isotope). Both electrons occupy the 1s orbital with opposite spin quantum numbers (m_s = +1/2 and -1/2), forming a closed shell. This configuration makes helium extremely stable and chemically inert — it has the highest ionization energy of any element (24.6 eV). The electron-electron repulsion makes an exact analytical solution impossible; the displayed orbital uses a hydrogen-like approximation with effective nuclear charge Z_eff ≈ 1.69. The drawn cloud uses Z_eff = 27/16 = 1.6875, so its 90% surface is at 2.66 a₀ / Z_eff = 83.5 pm.

equations.label: Pauli exclusion
equations.tex: No two fermions can share all quantum numbers (n, l, m, m_s)

simplifications: Each electron is drawn as a hydrogen-like 1s cloud with effective nuclear charge Z_eff = 27/16, which accounts for the electrons' repulsion only on average.
